scope_note: A password in the configuration is not the same as a password protecting something: type 7 reversibility, login with no password, and login local with no user database.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which value does R1 accept at the privileged EXEC prompt?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
enable password Harbour42
enable secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

options.text: Wr3nch-Harbour-42, because enable secret takes precedence.
Harbour42, because enable password is the older command and is read first.
Either value, since both commands populate the same credential store.
Neither, because configuring both together disables privileged access.

items.explanation: When both are present the secret always wins, and the older enable password is ignored entirely; the secret is also stored as a hash rather than recoverable text, which is why it replaced the earlier command. Option B assumes configuration order decides, when precedence is fixed regardless of where each line sits. Option C treats them as one store, but they are separate and only one is consulted. Option D invents a lockout that would make the pair impossible to configure safely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two conclusions should the reviewer draw now that the configuration has left the building? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
service password-encryption
!
username backup password 7 08701E1D5D4C53
username netadmin secret 9 $9$Xk2mQvR8LpT4c0$hV1nZ7yW3sK
!

The configuration was reviewed after a contractor was given a copy of it
for a documentation exercise.

options.text: The backup account's password can be recovered from the file as it stands.
service password-encryption has made both credentials safe to share.
The netadmin credential is stored as a hash and is not recoverable that way.
Both credentials are held as plain text and both must be changed.
The netadmin credential is the one at immediate risk of exposure.

items.explanation: Type 7 is an obfuscation rather than a hash and is reversed in seconds with freely available tools, so the backup password is effectively public, while the netadmin secret is stored as type 9, a genuine hash that does not give its input back. Option B treats service password-encryption as real protection, which is the misconception this item targets. Option D ignores the difference the two type numbers record. Option E reverses which of the two is exposed.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why are the credentials rejected on every attempt?

exhibit.content:
! R3 - relevant configuration
!
hostname R3
ip domain-name example.internal
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
!
enable secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

No engineer can log in over SSH. The connection is accepted and then the
credentials are rejected, whatever is typed.

options.text: The RSA key must be regenerated after the domain name is set.
login local checks a local user database, and no username is configured.
transport input ssh has to be paired with transport output ssh to work.
The enable secret has to be removed before local logins will be accepted.

items.explanation: login local tells the line to authenticate against locally configured usernames, and this configuration defines none, so every attempt fails no matter what is typed; adding a username with a secret resolves it. Option A reverses the ordering, since the domain name must exist before the key is generated and this configuration does that correctly. Option C invents a pairing requirement, as transport output governs outbound sessions from the device. Option D confuses the enable secret, which guards privileged mode after login rather than login itself.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this message indicate about the vty configuration?

exhibit.content:
R4(config)# line vty 0 4
R4(config-line)# login
R4(config-line)# transport input telnet
R4(config-line)# end
R4#

An engineer then tries to connect from a workstation:

    % Password required, but none set

    [Connection to 10.4.4.1 closed by foreign host]

options.text: The device is refusing Telnet because only SSH is permitted on those lines.
The vty lines have run out of free sessions and are turning connections away.
login was configured without a line password, so the device refuses access.
The connection was closed because no enable secret has been configured yet.

items.explanation: The plain login command tells the line to check a password configured on that line, and when none exists IOS refuses the session outright rather than letting anyone in unauthenticated, which is the safe behaviour and exactly what the message reports. Option A is contradicted by transport input telnet permitting the protocol used. Option B describes exhausted vty sessions, which produce a different refusal. Option D points at the enable secret, which is consulted only after a successful login.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which account can enter privileged EXEC mode without supplying a further credential?

exhibit.content:
R5# show running-config | include ^username
username helpdesk privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Lm4pQ2xR7vN9a0$cW8tY
username netadmin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$Kd7nB3wS5hJ2f0$pR6uX
username monitor privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Zq9cV4tG8mL1e0$nD3sA
username backup privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Rt5xH6yK2bF7d0$jM4wQ

options.text: netadmin
helpdesk
backup
monitor

items.explanation: Privilege level 15 places an account straight into privileged EXEC on login, and netadmin is the only one configured with it. Options B, C and D are all set to privilege 1, which lands them in user EXEC and requires the enable secret before they can go further. All four store their credential as type 9, so the difference between them is the privilege level rather than how the password is held.
